Three Blocks That Make Claude Get Smarter Every Session
I added three blocks to my CLAUDE.md a month ago. By week three, Claude was applying 24 project-specific rules it had written itself — rules I never prompted, extracted from patterns across dozens of sessions.
What This Article Demonstrates:
  • A Knowledge Architecture block that turns Claude into a system that learns across sessions — not just a tool that forgets
  • A Decision Journal block that logs every meaningful choice with full reasoning, so Claude (and your team) never re-debates settled decisions
  • A Quality Gate block that gives Claude concrete evaluation criteria — because agents can’t objectively judge their own work
  • A schedule suggestion that keeps the whole system from going stale

0. Memory Without Reflection

Claude remembers everything. It writes its own memories, reads your CLAUDE.md, follows your conventions across sessions.
But it doesn't learn.
It captured that your pricing test showed 40% churn. It captured that a competitor dropped their free tier. It captured that onboarding users churned less. Three separate observations in three separate sessions — and Claude never connected them.
Memory without reflection is just storage. And most CLAUDE.md setups are exactly that — a growing correction log that never promotes patterns, never tests its own hypotheses, never evaluates whether the work actually meets your standards.
I spent a month fixing this with three blocks. By week three, Claude was applying 24 project-specific rules it had written itself — rules I never prompted, extracted from patterns across dozens of sessions.
Each block targets a different failure mode. Here's the thinking behind them.

1. Knowledge Architecture — The Learning Loop

The failure mode: Claude captures observations but never revisits them. Insights from last week don't inform this week's work. There's no mechanism to test whether a pattern holds, promote it when it does, or discard it when it doesn't.
The principle: Force active retrieval before every task. Claude reads existing knowledge before making recommendations. Then after the task, extract what was learned and store it in domain-specific folders with a clear hierarchy: raw observations, hypotheses that need more data, and confirmed rules that get applied by default.
The key mechanism is the promotion cycle. An observation starts as a hypothesis. When it gets confirmed across multiple sessions, it becomes a rule. When new data contradicts a rule, it gets demoted back. The system self-corrects instead of accumulating stale advice.
After a month, I had a folder where Claude had promoted 24 rules on its own. I didn't write them. They emerged from dozens of sessions. Claude was measurably better — not because of better prompts, but because the system had been learning the whole time.

2. Decision Journal — Reviewable Reasoning

The failure mode: Someone asks why you picked Postgres over DynamoDB. Or why you killed the freemium tier. Nobody remembers. So you spend 30 minutes re-debating a decision that was already made.
The principle: Before making any significant decision, Claude searches for prior decisions in that area first. If one exists, it follows the existing reasoning unless new information invalidates it. If no prior decision exists, it logs the full context — what was decided, what else was on the table, why this option won, what trade-offs were accepted.
If you've worked with Architecture Decision Records, this will feel familiar — same principle, enforced by Claude instead of team discipline (good luck enforcing the latter).
The part that surprised me: when decisions get replaced, the journal creates a traceable chain. You can see reasoning evolve over time. And the decisions I was most confident about had the worst hit rate. The ones where I forced myself to think through alternatives were right 80% of the time.

3. Quality Gate — Evaluation Criteria That Compound

The failure mode: Claude finishes a task and tells you it's done. You ask if the work is good. Claude says yes — confidently, every time. Anthropic's own engineering team documented this: agents confidently praise work they produced, even when the quality is mediocre. The agent that built the thing can't objectively judge the thing.
The principle: Give Claude concrete, testable evaluation criteria specific to your project. Not vague aspirations like "be thorough" — specific checks like "churn impact modeled for both monthly and annual cohorts" or "edge cases documented for each user flow."
The criteria evolve. When a check catches a real issue, it gets noted. When a check keeps catching the same class of problem, it gets promoted to an automatic gate. When a check has never triggered across many evaluations, it gets flagged for pruning. The quality bar tightens around your actual failure patterns instead of staying frozen.
If you've worked with Definition of Done in Scrum, this is that — but it gets sharper every week instead of gathering dust in a wiki.

How They Reinforce Each Other

The blocks aren't independent. Quality Gate catches a pattern — Knowledge Architecture promotes it to a rule. A decision ages badly — the journal gets a replacement entry with full context on why the reasoning changed. Knowledge rules shape future decisions. Criteria feed back into knowledge.
You paste three blocks. The system builds itself from your actual work.
One more piece keeps it sharp: a maintenance schedule. Instructions that tells Claude to periodically suggest a system review — prune stale rules, check if hypotheses have enough evidence to promote, review whether trade-offs played out as expected, flag criteria that stopped being useful.
Claude suggests the review. You decide when to run it.

The Full System

The principles above are the architecture. The implementation is three paste-in blocks for your CLAUDE.md plus a schedule suggestion — ready to drop in and working by your next session.
